title: Itsekiri Banga Soup
author: Oritsegbemi Okoh
desc: The cold-water extraction — palm fruit boiled thirty minutes, pounded, then squeezed with cold water — and catfish set in undisturbed for exactly seven minutes.
longDesc: This is banga as the Itsekiri make it, and it differs from the Urhobo version in one step that the source itself calls diagnostic: the cream is extracted with cold water rather than just-boiled. Palm fruit boils thirty minutes until the flesh softens, is pounded to separate flesh from seeds, then squeezed by hand with cold water and strained to give about three cups of thick orange cream. The fish goes in at the end on a strict schedule — catfish undisturbed for seven minutes, shrimp for the final three — and the finished soup should coat the back of a spoon.
ingredients: 2 lbs fresh palm fruit, or 3 cups tinned palm fruit concentrate
1.5 lbs fresh catfish, cleaned and cut into medium pieces
1/2 lb fresh shrimp, deveined and rinsed
1/2 lb smoked fish, deboned and broken into chunks
// Banga spice blend — quantities not specified in the source
steps: If using fresh palm fruits, boil them in water for 30 minutes until the flesh softens. Pound in a mortar to separate the flesh from the seeds. Add cold water and squeeze the flesh by hand to extract the cream. Strain through a sieve — you should get about 3 cups of thick, orange cream.
Bring the cream to the boil, stirring occasionally to prevent separation, and simmer 15 minutes until it thickens slightly.
Add the diced onion and scotch bonnets and simmer 10 minutes.
Drop in the oburunbebe sticks and irugeje seeds. Sprinkle in the ground beletete and ataiko.
Add the ground and whole dried crayfish and cook 10 minutes.
Add the smoked fish and seasoning cubes and cook 5 minutes.
Place the catfish pieces into the soup gently. Do not stir — let the fish sit in the simmering cream and cook undisturbed for 7 minutes.
Add the shrimp for the final 3 minutes. Shrimp overcook quickly and turn rubbery if left too long.
The soup should be rich, creamy and aromatic, and it should coat the back of a spoon. If it is too thick, add a splash of warm water.
Serve with starch. Tear off a piece, dip it generously into the soup, and swallow.
chefTips: Cold water for the extraction, and the source says this is what distinguishes the Itsekiri method from the Igbo one. The Urhobo version pours just-boiled water over the bruised nuts instead.
Thirty minutes on the palm fruit boil, against fifteen to twenty in the Urhobo account. Both are stated by named sources and neither is adjusted here.
Seven minutes undisturbed for the catfish. Do not stir, do not turn, do not look at it. Catfish falls apart if handled.
Three minutes for the shrimp and no more. The source's reason is exact: shrimp overcook quickly and turn rubbery.
Coats the back of a spoon is the consistency cue, and it is a good one for a soup this rich.
Stir occasionally while the cream first boils, to prevent it separating. After that, as little stirring as possible.
Total time is about eighty minutes including the extraction. If you start from the tin, take an hour off.
commonMistakes: Using hot water for the extraction, which is the Urhobo rather than the Itsekiri method.
Stirring after the catfish goes in.
Leaving the shrimp in longer than three minutes.
Letting the cream separate at the first boil.
Serving it thin enough to run off the spoon.
sources: Adapted from 'Banga Soup: The Itsekiri Palm Nut Soup — Recipe & Cultural Guide', byline 'INC-USA Editorial', Itsekiri National Congress USA, dated April 2026.

CAVEAT, STATED PLAINLY. This is a named institution — a 501(c)(3) ethnic association — which meets the named-source bar, but the byline is editorial rather than individual, the date is recent, and the recipe uses US customary units (lbs, cups) for a Niger Delta dish, which together suggest recently written editorial copy rather than directly transmitted practice. It is used here because it is the only Itsekiri-institutional source found, and because its spice glossary is specific enough to be worth having. Weight it accordingly.

Quantities as printed, for six servings: 2 lbs fresh palm fruit (or 3 cups tinned palm fruit concentrate); 1.5 lbs fresh catfish; 1/2 lb fresh shrimp; 1/2 lb smoked fish; 3 tablespoons ground crayfish; 1/4 cup whole dried crayfish; Banga spice blend (beletete, oburunbebe, ataiko, irugeje) — quantities explicitly not specified on the page; 2 Scotch bonnet peppers; 1 medium onion; 2 seasoning cubes; salt to taste; starch (usi) for serving. Total cook time stated: about 80 minutes including extraction.

All times and cues are as printed, including the 30-minute boil, the cold-water extraction, the ~3 cups of cream, the 15-minute simmer, the 10 minutes with onion and pepper, the 10 minutes with crayfish, the 5 minutes with smoked fish, the catfish 'undisturbed for 7 minutes', the shrimp 'for the final 3 minutes' with the reason given, and the consistency cue 'It should coat the back of a spoon.'

THE EXTRACTION DISAGREEMENT, not reconciled, and this source names it as diagnostic: it contrasts banga with Igbo ofe akwu on extraction method, cold against hot. The Kitchen Butterfly account pours just-boiled water over the bruised nuts (NGA043). Direct opposition on a step one source says tells the two traditions apart.

THE SPICE GLOSSARY, verbatim and the most useful content on the page: on beletete — 'Beletete (sometimes spelled "beletentien") is a dried leaf with a warm, aromatic fragrance somewhere between bay leaf and dried basil, but more complex.' On oburunbebe — 'Oburunbebe is a dried stick — literally a piece of bark or woody stem — that adds a subtle bitterness and depth.' On the blend as a whole — 'Without these four spices, you have a palm nut stew — with them, you have banga.'

On the name, as printed: 'The word "banga" comes from the Itsekiri and Urhobo languages, referring to the palm fruit from which the soup base is extracted.' On the pairing: 'Banga soup is always served with starch (usi) — a fermented cassava swallow that is unique to the Niger Delta.' On occasion: 'At every Itsekiri celebration, from Temotsi weddings to funeral rites, banga soup served with starch announces: this is an Itsekiri table.'

LIMITATION FLAGGED: the page places banga among the Itsekiri, Urhobo, Isoko and Ijaw and distinguishes it from Igbo ofe akwu, but it does NOT differentiate the Itsekiri version from the Urhobo or Isoko ones — which is the distinction an Itsekiri source would most usefully supply.

Its claim that usi is 'a fermented cassava swallow' conflicts with the Kitchen Butterfly cassava guide, which describes starch as a settled slurry and does not list fermentation among its steps. See NGA042.
GAP: amiedi, the Urhobo name for the palm-nut preparation, appears in no named-source recipe found. It is attested as a name in passing and no priority source publishes a recipe under it.
storage: 4 days refrigerated. Remove the shrimp before freezing.
reheating: Gentle heat, lid off, no stirring once warm.
healthBenefits: Catfish and shrimp are both very lean, high-quality proteins.
Palm nut pulp is rich in carotenoids and tocotrienols.
High in iodine, selenium and omega-3 fats.
culturalNote: Banga with starch is, by this source's account, what announces an Itsekiri table — served at Temotsi weddings, at funeral rites, at naming ceremonies and chieftaincy installations. The word banga itself comes from the Itsekiri and Urhobo languages and refers to the palm fruit, which is why the soup carries different names everywhere else and that one everywhere the fruit is called that.
